docs.title: oboromi
docs.text:
This is the documentation of oboromi, an early Nintendo Switch 2 emulator written in Rust. An emulator is a program that lets a PC act like the console. It builds on the foundations its maintainer and contributors laid down. Most of the recent work is on the graphics chip, the GPU, with the CPU, services and audio in progress.

A game hands the Switch 2's GPU small programs called shaders, for example one that computes the colour of each pixel of a sky. Those shaders are NVIDIA machine code. The emulator rewrites them into SPIR-V, the shader format of the cross-vendor graphics API Vulkan. Then an Intel, AMD or NVIDIA card in a PC can run them.

The Demo button: a hand-written SM86 program, translated to SPIR-V, redrawing a Julia set every frame on an Intel laptop GPU.

Start here For Architecture map One picture of the whole emulator, and which page answers what Decision records The big design choices, each explained in plain words first Glossary Every GPU term the pages use, with one plain sentence and an example SM86 instruction table (PDF) Every instruction encoding of the Switch 2's GPU, generated from NVIDIA's table

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
A game talks to its GPU through command words in memory and small programs called shaders. Each piece on that path has its own name. For example, to draw a triangle the game writes a command list and points the GPU at it. The GPU then runs a shader for every covered pixel.

flowchart LR
    GPFIFO["GPFIFO<br/>Queue of pointers to command lists"] --> PB["Pushbuffer<br/>One command list in memory"] --> M["Methods<br/>Single register writes"]
    M --> C3["3D class<br/>Drawing settings: shaders, constants, textures"]
    M --> CC["Compute class<br/>Compute launches, described by a QMD"]
    C3 --> SASS["SASS<br/>NVIDIA shader machine code"]
    CC --> SASS
    SASS -->|"Translator"| SPIRV["SPIR-V<br/>The shader format Vulkan runs"]

How a game's commands lead to shader code a PC's GPU can run.

docs.title: Chips and code formats
docs.text: Term What it is Example GPU The graphics chip: many small cores running the same program on many pixels or numbers at once. Shading every pixel of a frame in parallel. Guest, host The guest is the emulated Switch 2 and its memory; the host is the PC running oboromi. A guest address points into emulated console RAM. Shader A small program the GPU runs once per vertex, pixel or work item. A pixel shader that returns one pixel's colour. SASS NVIDIA's native GPU machine code, the instructions the chip really executes. FADD R0, R1, R2 adds two floats; on SM86 each instruction is a 128-bit word. SM86 The instruction set of NVIDIA's Ampere desktop chips, which the Switch 2 also uses. An RTX 3090 runs SM86 code. SM88 CUDA's name for the Switch 2 GPU's instruction set; its encoding table equals SM86's. nvdisasm --binary SM88 decodes Switch 2 code. Ampere NVIDIA's GPU generation shared by desktop cards and the Switch 2. RTX 30 series cards are Ampere. T239 The Switch 2's system-on-chip: ARM CPU cores plus an Ampere GPU called GA10F. The main chip inside every Switch 2. GA102 The desktop Ampere chip the reference results are recorded on. RTX 3090 and RTX A6000 are GA102 cards. Silicon Real hardware, as opposed to an emulator or a CPU-based driver. "matches silicon" means an RTX 3090 gave the same bytes. SPIR-V The binary shader format Vulkan accepts, like bytecode for GPUs. The translator writes one SPIR-V module per guest program. Module One SPIR-V program, ready to hand to a Vulkan driver. The translated Julia demo shader. Translator oboromi's code that rewrites SASS into SPIR-V. core/src/gpu/sm86. Encoding class One row of NVIDIA's instruction table: a bit pattern plus its fields. An add with a register operand and one with a constant are two classes. Handler The translator function that emits SPIR-V for one instruction family. The FADD handler emits a float add. Opcode The name of an instruction. IMAD is integer multiply-add.

docs.title: How commands reach the GPU
docs.text: Term What it is Example Channel One stream of commands from a program to the GPU. A game's renderer usually owns one. GPFIFO A ring of small entries, each pointing at a pushbuffer and giving its length. The game appends one entry per batch of commands. Pushbuffer A list of 32-bit command words in guest memory: a header word, then data words. "set viewport width to 1920" is one header and one data word. Method One register write to a GPU engine, named by its register offset. Writing the vertex count before a draw. Class A GPU engine's set of registers, identified by a number. 0xC797 is the Ampere 3D engine, 0xC7C0 compute, 0xC76F the channel. Subchannel One of eight slots a channel binds a class into, so each header can pick an engine. Subchannel 0 holds the 3D class after SET_OBJECT. SET_OBJECT The channel method that binds a class to a subchannel. Sent once at the start of a command stream. Draw trigger The method write that means "draw now with the current settings". DRAW_VERTEX_ARRAY_BEGIN_END_INSTANCE_FIRST. Snapshot A frozen copy of the GPU settings at the moment of a draw or launch. DrawSnapshot holds the viewport the draw used. Semaphore A memory word the GPU writes or waits on, to tell the CPU how far it got. A release writes a counter when a frame is done. Syncpoint The Switch's hardware counter for the same job, managed by the OS. The display waits on one before showing a frame. Report A value the GPU writes to memory on request. A counter or timestamp after a draw. MME, MME64 A small macro processor in the GPU that expands one call into many method writes. One macro call that sets up a whole draw. QMD Queue meta data: a block in guest memory describing one compute launch. Grid size, threads per group, program address, constant buffers. Dispatch One compute launch: run a program over a grid of threads. One dispatch per frame of the Julia demo.

docs.title: Shaders and their data
docs.text: Term What it is Example Stage Which step of drawing a shader belongs to. Vertex, fragment or compute. Vertex shader Runs once per corner of a triangle and computes where it lands on screen. Multiplying a position by the camera matrix. Fragment shader Runs once per covered pixel and computes its colour; also called a pixel shader. Sampling a texture and returning the colour. Compute shader A shader not tied to drawing, run over a grid of threads for general work. The Julia set demo. SPH Shader program header: a block before a graphics program naming its stage, inputs and outputs. "vertex stage, writes position and one colour". IMAP, OMAP The SPH's input and output maps: which attributes a shader reads and writes. OMAP bit for "writes generic attribute 0". Attribute A per-vertex value passed between stages. Position, colour or texture coordinate. Interpolation Blending a vertex value across a triangle's pixels; "flat" means no blending. A colour fading from one corner to another. cbuf Constant buffer: a small read-only table of numbers the game hands the shader. The camera matrix, read as c[bank][offset]. Bank Which of a shader's constant buffers an access names. Bank 0 carries launch data in compute, such as the grid size. Global memory The GPU's view of main memory, read and written by address. LDG loads from it, STG stores to it. Shared memory A small fast scratch area shared by the threads of one workgroup. Threads swapping partial sums. Local memory Per-thread scratch memory for values that do not fit in registers. A large per-thread array. Register A named per-thread variable inside the GPU core. R0 to R253; RZ always reads zero. Predicate A one-bit register that decides whether an instruction runs. @P0 FADD adds only where P0 is true. Uniform datapath Per-warp registers holding one value shared by all its threads. UR0 to UR62 and predicates UP0 to UP6. pc Program counter: the position of the next instruction. A branch sets the pc to its target. Basic block A run of instructions entered only at the top and left only at the bottom. The body of a loop without inner branches. Attribute space The address range an instruction uses to name an attribute. Position sits at 0x70.

docs.title: How the GPU runs threads
docs.text: Term What it is Example Thread, invocation, lane One running copy of a shader; Vulkan says invocation, and a lane is a thread's slot in a warp. The thread shading one pixel. Warp A team of threads that runs one instruction stream in lockstep. NVIDIA warps are 32 threads. Subgroup Vulkan's name for a warp; its width depends on the device. lavapipe's subgroups are 8 wide. Workgroup A group of threads that can share memory and wait for each other; CUDA calls it a block. 256 threads working on one tile of an image. Divergence Threads of one warp taking different sides of a branch. Pixels inside and outside a circle. Reconvergence The point where diverged threads join up again. The end of an if-else. BSSY, BSYNC The SM86 instruction pair marking where diverged threads of a warp join again. BSSY before an if, BSYNC after it. Barrier A point every thread of a group must reach before any goes on. BAR before reading what others wrote to shared memory. Collective An instruction where threads of a warp exchange values. VOTE asks which threads have a condition; SHFL reads a teammate's register. Structured control flow SPIR-V's rule that branches must form nested loops and ifs, with no free jumps. No goto into the middle of a loop.

docs.title: Textures
docs.text: Term What it is Example Texture An image a shader reads with filtering. A brick wall image on a model. Sampler The settings for reading a texture: edge wrapping, filtering, level of detail. Repeat at the edges, smooth between pixels. TIC Texture image control: a header describing one texture's format, size, layout, address and mip levels. One 32-byte entry per texture. TSC Texture sampler control: an entry holding one sampler's settings. One 32-byte entry per sampler. Pool A table of TIC or TSC entries in guest memory. A game's texture pool with hundreds of headers. Handle A cbuf word that picks one TIC entry and one TSC entry. Low 20 bits pick the texture, top 12 bits the sampler. Mip level A smaller copy of the same texture, used when it appears far away. A 512 pixel texture with 256, 128 and smaller copies. LOD Level of detail: which mip level a read uses. LOD 0 is full size. Format How a pixel's bytes are laid out. A8B8G8R8 is four 8-bit channels; BC1, BC3, BC7 are compressed. sRGB A colour encoding matching how screens show brightness, decoded to linear before maths. Most photos and base-colour textures. Pitch-linear Plain rows of pixels, one after another. A screenshot in memory. Block-linear NVIDIA's tiled layout that keeps nearby pixels close in memory. Most textures a game uploads. GOB Group of bytes: the small tile block-linear layouts are built from. 64 bytes wide and 8 rows high. Deswizzle Reorder tiled pixels back into plain rows. Turning a block-linear texture into a Vulkan image. Surface An image a shader writes pixel by pixel instead of sampling; Vulkan calls it a storage image. SUST stores one pixel. Render target The image a draw writes its pixels into. A colour image plus an optional depth image. Index buffer A list of vertex numbers saying which vertices form each triangle, so shared corners are stored once. A square as four vertices and six indices. Instancing Drawing the same mesh many times in one call, with per-copy data such as position. A thousand particles in one draw. Blending Mixing a new pixel's colour with the one already in the image. A see-through window over a wall. Window origin Whether screen y counts from the top or the bottom row of the image. OpenGL-style games count from the bottom. Depth Per-pixel distance, used to hide what is behind. A wall in front of a door.

docs.title: Tensor cores
docs.text: Term What it is Example Tensor core A unit that multiplies small matrices in one instruction. AI inference and upscaling use them. HMMA, IMMA Matrix multiply-accumulate on tensor cores, for half-precision floats and for integers. One HMMA computes D = A × B + C across a warp. DMMA, BMMA The same for double-precision floats and for single bits. DMMA for scientific maths. LDSM, MOVM Load and rearrange matrix pieces for tensor instructions. Loading a tile from shared memory. Matrix fragment The part of a matrix one thread holds. A few elements of row 3 of A. TF32 A reduced-precision float format tensor cores use for speed. 32 bits of storage, fewer mantissa bits used. Truncation Dropping low bits instead of rounding them. 1.27 truncated to one decimal is 1.2. IEEE order Adding numbers one at a time, rounding after each step, as standard float rules do. ((a + b) + c) + d.

docs.title: Vulkan
docs.text: Term What it is Example Vulkan The cross-vendor API programs use to drive a GPU. The same code runs on Intel, AMD and NVIDIA. ICD Installable client driver: the library that gives Vulkan a device. lavapipe's ICD file. Queue Where a program submits work to the GPU. One queue that takes both graphics and compute. Command buffer A recorded list of GPU commands submitted in one go. "bind pipeline, dispatch, copy back". Fence A flag the GPU sets when submitted work finishes, so the CPU can wait. Waiting for a dispatch before reading its output. Pipeline A compiled bundle of shaders plus fixed settings, needed before any draw or dispatch. Vertex shader, fragment shader, vertex layout and colour format. Dynamic state Settings that can change per draw without building a new pipeline. Viewport and cull mode. Dynamic rendering Drawing straight into images, without Vulkan's older render pass objects. One call names the colour and depth images. Descriptor A small record telling a shader where one buffer or image is. "binding 33 is this buffer". Binding A numbered slot a shader reads a resource from; the host plugs a buffer or image into it. Binding 9 holds the global memory window. Descriptor set A group of bindings plugged in together. oboromi uses only set 0. Uniform buffer A small read-only buffer behind a binding. A guest cbuf. Storage buffer, SSBO A large buffer a shader can read and write. The global memory window. std140 Vulkan's layout rule for uniform buffers, which pads each array element to 16 bytes. Why cbufs are declared as uvec4 arrays. uvec4 Four 32-bit unsigned integers, 16 bytes in total. One row of a cbuf array. Resource list The bindings a translated module declares, with what each one holds. "binding 1 is cbuf 0, binding 36 is the texture at cbuf 0 offset 0x10". Validation layer A Vulkan debug layer that reports misuse of the API. Catching an image used in the wrong layout. spirv-val The Khronos tool that checks a SPIR-V module is valid. It rejected a compute shader that used OpKill. lavapipe Mesa's Vulkan driver that runs on the CPU, also called llvmpipe. The device in CI. DontUnroll A SPIR-V hint asking the driver not to copy a loop body out. Keeps a four-pass loop as a loop. Inlining A compiler pasting a function's body into every caller. A helper function vanishing from the compiled code. Register spill Moving values to slower memory when a program needs more registers than the core has. Intel spilling in the tensor loops. Readback Copying results from GPU memory back to CPU memory. Reading a frame's pixels after a draw. Denormal A tiny float close to zero that some hardware flushes to zero. 1e-40 as a 32-bit float. NaN "not a number", the float result of an invalid operation. 0.0 / 0.0.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text: Term What it is Example VA, PA GPU virtual address, which shaders use, and guest-physical address, where the bytes sit in emulated RAM. One VA can be repointed to another PA. Page The fixed-size chunk the address map works in. 64 KiB here. Page map The table that turns GPU virtual pages into guest-physical pages. PageMap in memory.rs. Remap Pointing a GPU address at different memory. A game moving a vertex buffer. Aliasing Two addresses sharing the same memory. A texture that is also a render target. Mirror A host copy of a guest buffer, kept for Vulkan. The vertex buffer copy a draw reads. Generation A counter stamped on each page write, so a copy can tell it is stale. A mirror refreshes when its pages' generation moved. Coherence Keeping all copies of the same data in agreement. The CPU seeing the pixels a draw wrote. Global memory window One storage buffer holding the guest memory range a program can touch. The output image of the gradient program. Memory descriptor An extra policy word the compiler attaches to some loads and stores; it is not part of the address. LDG.E desc[UR4][R2.64].

docs.title: The rest of the emulator
docs.text: Term What it is Example Unicorn The CPU emulator library oboromi's ARM cores run on, built on QEMU's CPU core. It executes AArch64 instructions. QEMU The open-source machine emulator whose CPU core Unicorn reuses. It also runs whole ARM Linux systems. Cortex-A78C The Arm CPU core in the Switch 2's chip. Eight of them in the T239. switchbrew The community wiki that documents the Switch's system calls, services and hardware. Its NV services page. libnx The homebrew library for writing Switch programs. Its request layout is what the guest's encoder follows. AArch64 The 64-bit ARM instruction set the Switch 2's CPU runs. The game's main code. FFI Foreign function interface: the Rust functions the C++ Qt window calls. ffi.rs. HLE High-level emulation: writing a firmware service's behaviour instead of running its code. Answering a "get time" call directly. Service An OS process a game talks to. nvdrv is the GPU driver service, vi the display service. HIPC The Switch's message format for calling services. A header plus arguments in a buffer. SVC Supervisor call: a system call into the Switch kernel. Mapping memory. Ioctl A control call into a driver. An nvdrv call that allocates GPU memory. nvmap, host1x The Switch's GPU memory allocator and its sync and DMA unit. nvmap hands out buffer handles. NSO, NRO Switch executable file formats. A game's main program is an NSO. Loader The code that places a game's executable in memory and starts it. The flat-image loader for our own guest program. Session An open connection from a game to one service. A session with nvdrv. Handle A number the kernel gives a program to name something it opened. The session handle SendSyncRequest takes. Port A named address a program connects to in order to open a session. The port named nvdrv. IPC Inter-process communication: one program sending a message to another. A game asking the display service for a layer. IPC buffer A small per-thread memory area that holds the request and then the reply. The request bytes for SendSyncRequest. CMIF The command layer on top of HIPC: a magic word, a command id and arguments. SFCI, then command 1, then the ioctl number. Transfer memory Guest memory a program lends to a service. The audio renderer's work buffer. Driver fence A sync counter value a program waits on to know its GPU work finished. The fence SubmitGpfifo returns. Binder The display's messaging layer, inherited from Android, for handing over frames. QueueBuffer through IHOSBinderDriver. Turn lock The lock that lets either the CPU or the GPU use guest RAM, never both. The GPU takes it before a draw. Write hook A Unicorn callback that runs on every guest store to a chosen range. Marking pages the GPU must refresh.

docs.title: Tools, tests and references
docs.text:
Term What it is Example nvdisasm NVIDIA's disassembler; the decoder is generated from the instruction table it carries. Turning a 128-bit word into FADD R0, R1, R2. nvcc NVIDIA's CUDA compiler. nvcc -arch=sm_86 -cubin kernel.cu. CUDA NVIDIA's way of writing general GPU programs in C++. A kernel that adds two arrays. Kernel A CUDA program launched over a grid of threads. The mul-add test kernel. cubin An ELF file holding compiled CUDA kernels for one SM version. kernels.cubin. libcuda NVIDIA's driver library that runs CUDA programs on its cards. libcuda.so.1. Capture One recording of an instruction run on a real card: inputs, instruction, outputs. An integer add with its result registers. Fixture A stored test case, here usually a capture. One line of sm86-thread.jsonl. Scoreboard test A test that replays every capture and fails on any unlisted mismatch. fixtures_match_silicon. Seed kernel A small compiled CUDA program used as a carrier for one patched instruction. cuda-seed.cu. Ryujinx An open-source Switch 1 emulator whose GPU code is a reference. Its texture size calculator. NAK Mesa's open-source shader compiler for NVIDIA GPUs. Its shader header layout. Open-gpu-doc NVIDIA's public hardware headers. clc797.h, the 3D class registers. Mesa The open-source graphics driver stack on Linux. It ships lavapipe. glTF A standard 3D model file format. The BoomBox sample model. PBR Physically based rendering: lighting that follows real material behaviour. Metal and rough surfaces lit by one light. Voice One playing sound in the audio renderer. A footstep sample with its volume and pitch. Mix A bus that voices or other mixes add into. All sound effects together. Sink Where the audio renderer's final sound goes. The device sink, the speakers. ADPCM A compressed sample format the Switch's audio uses. Music stored at a quarter of its PCM size. Biquad A small audio filter that cuts or boosts some frequencies. A low-pass to muffle a sound behind a wall. Ray query A shader asking "what does this ray hit first?" against the scene. A shadow ray from a pixel towards the light. Acceleration structure A search tree over a scene's triangles that makes ray queries fast. Built once per model, then queried per pixel.

Sources: core/src/gpu/{fifo,threed,texture,engine}.rs, core/src/gpu/compute_class.rs on gpu/qmd-dispatch, NVIDIA's open-gpu-doc class headers.

docs.title: Decision records
docs.text:
A decision record, or ADR, explains one design choice: the problem, the choice, and what it costs. Each one opens with a short "In plain words" section, then the details. For example, ADR-0004 explains why emulated RAM is the one true copy of all data.

ADR Decision 0001 Every shader finds its data in one fixed table of numbered slots 0002 Game memory reaches a shader through one window buffer 0003 Threads that take different branches run in turns 0004 Emulated RAM is the one true copy; host copies check a write counter 0005 Matrix sums copy the chip exactly, written as small loops 0006 GPU commands run one after another, each draw with frozen settings 0007 The Switch 2 chip decodes with the desktop instruction table 0008 Real chips are the reference, known differences are listed per device

Each record follows the MADR template and names its component in the front matter.

docs.title: Every shader finds its data in a fixed table of numbered slots
In plain words
docs.text: A Vulkan shader cannot follow a pointer to its data. Instead it reads from numbered slots, and before each run the host plugs a buffer or an image into each slot. Think of a patch panel: the shader asks for a socket by number and reads whatever is plugged in there. We fixed the socket numbers once, for every shader, so the host always knows what goes where.

docs.title: Context and Problem Statement
docs.text: A translated shader needs several kinds of data: our own helper values, the game's constant tables, the game's main memory, and any number of textures. Compute shaders and drawing shaders must agree on which slot holds what. A vertex shader and a pixel shader drawing together may each want their own buffer in the same slot.

docs.title: Decision Outcome
docs.text:
Vulkan calls a slot a binding and a group of slots a descriptor set. Compute and vertex shaders use set 0. Pixel shaders use set 1, with the same slot numbers. Each set holds these slots:

Binding Vulkan kind Holds 0 Uniform buffer: small, read-only Our helper values, today the start address of the memory window; never game data 1 to 32 Uniform buffers The game's constant buffers 0 to 31, all the banks a stage has 33 Storage buffer: large, read-write The window onto the game's main memory, see ADR-0002 34, 35 Storage buffers Register values in and out, for tests only 36 and up Image slots Textures and writable images, numbered in the order the shader first uses them

A constant buffer, or cbuf, is a small read-only table of numbers the game hands the shader, such as the camera matrix. Vulkan's layout rule for uniform buffers, std140, pads each array element to a fixed width. A uvec4 is exactly that width, so each cbuf is declared as a uvec4 array and no space is wasted.

Layout fact Value std140 array element Padded to 16 bytes uvec4 Four 32-bit words, 16 bytes

Two texture reads whose handle comes from the same cbuf word share one slot. A shader declares only the slots it uses. That list, its resource list, tells the host exactly what to plug in.

docs.title: What this makes easy
docs.text:
• One piece of host code, Descriptors, plugs in data for compute and for both drawing stages.
  • Our helper values can never be confused with what the game put in its first constant buffer.
  • A draw's vertex and pixel shaders can read different buffers through the same cbuf slot, because each has its own set.

docs.title: What this makes hard
docs.text:
• Every draw binds two sets instead of one, and the host must keep them apart.
  • Shaders that pick a texture by a run-time index will need arrays of slots next to this layout.

docs.title: Confirmation
docs.text:
Checked by spirv-val on every module, the Vulkan validation layer on dispatch and draw, and the texture tests that bind several images at once.

Sources: core/src/gpu/sm86/mod.rs, core/src/gpu/compute.rs.

docs.title: Game memory reaches a shader through one window buffer
In plain words
docs.text: Game shaders read memory by address, like a pointer in C. A Vulkan shader cannot use those addresses, because they point into the emulated console, not into the PC. So before each run the host copies the stretch of game memory the program may touch into one buffer, the window. The shader turns each game address into a position in that window by subtracting the window's start.

docs.title: Context and Problem Statement
docs.text: SASS loads and stores use the game's own GPU addresses. Vulkan shaders cannot follow those. Vulkan's own shader pointers, buffer device addresses, point into host memory and know nothing about the game's address map.

docs.title: Decision Outcome
docs.text:
All main memory a run touches, called global memory, is one storage buffer at binding 33. A storage buffer is a large buffer a shader can read and write.

The host looks the game's address range up in the page map, the table from GPU addresses to emulated RAM. It copies that range into one buffer and stores the window's start address in the helper slot, binding 0. For a compute launch from a command list, the range is all mapped guest memory. After the run, the pages the program changed are written back to guest RAM.

Window fact Value Start address Rounded down to a 16-byte boundary Widest access 128 bits Window for a launch from a command list All mapped guest memory, at most 4 GiB

A translated LDG (load from global memory) or STG (store) subtracts the start and indexes the buffer. An address outside mapped memory fails with an error. Buffer device addresses are not used.

docs.title: What this makes easy
docs.text:
• One rule covers every load, store and atomic, at any width the chip has.
  • A missing mapping is a clear error instead of a read of random memory.

docs.title: What this makes hard
docs.text:
• The window must hold every byte the program might touch, so the first launch copies all mapped memory to the card; later launches only copy pages that changed.
  • Some loads carry a memory descriptor, an extra policy word from the compiler, and it must not be added to the address.

docs.title: Confirmation
docs.text:
The compiled mul-add kernel and the gradient program match the real card through this window. The engine test runs the gradient kernel from a QMD launch and finds its output in guest memory. The memory tests cover remaps.

Sources: core/src/gpu/memory.rs window, core/src/gpu/sm86/access.rs, core/src/tests/gpu/harness.rs run_grid.

docs.title: In plain words
docs.text: The GPU runs threads in teams called warps. When teammates take different branches, the real chip parks some, runs the others, and joins them back later. Some instructions make teammates swap values, so they must be at the same place at the same time. We run such programs in turns: each turn, the teammates furthest behind take one step while the rest wait. It is like a tour group where the stragglers always walk next, so everyone meets at every stop.

docs.title: Context and Problem Statement
docs.text: The translator runs each thread as a loop over its own program counter, the pc. Collectives, instructions where teammates swap values such as VOTE and SHFL, need every thread to reach the same Vulkan barrier together. So does BAR, the chip's own barrier. With threads at different pcs that is undefined behaviour, and votes by part of a warp could not be reproduced.

docs.title: Considered Options
docs.text:
• Rebuild the game's jumps as nested Vulkan loops and ifs.
  • Use only Vulkan's subgroups, its own name for warps.
  • Keep the pc loop, and run it in turns across the whole thread group.

docs.title: Decision Outcome
docs.text:
Keep the pc loop. A program with collectives or BAR moves every thread of its group, the workgroup, together. Each turn the group votes for the lowest pc any thread waits at. Threads at that pc run one step, and the rest sit out with their memory writes masked.

BSSY and BSYNC, the chip's "rejoin here" markers, are tracked per thread. BAR arrivals are counted per barrier until all the required threads arrive. Programs without collectives keep the free per-thread loop. Swapping values through shared memory is the one method on every device.

Device fact Value NVIDIA warp width 32 threads Subgroup width on lavapipe 8 threads

docs.title: What this makes easy
docs.text:
• Votes, shuffles and barriers after a branch match the real chip, including votes by part of a warp.
  • It runs on lavapipe, whose subgroups are narrower than a warp.

docs.title: What this makes hard
docs.text:
• Programs with collectives pay a vote and a barrier on every step.
  • Whether a thread spinning in a wait loop ever lets the others move is not verified.

docs.title: Confirmation
docs.text:
The warp scoreboard passes on Intel and lavapipe, and tests cover branches of unequal length, nested markers and early exit.

Sources: core/src/gpu/sm86/mod.rs translate_program, core/src/gpu/sm86/warp.rs.

docs.title: Emulated RAM is the one true copy of all data
In plain words
docs.text: Vulkan cannot read the emulated console's RAM directly, so the emulator keeps PC-side copies of game data. Copies can go stale: the game might move a buffer, change it from the CPU, or draw into memory it later reads as a texture. So emulated RAM is the only truth. Every copy remembers where it came from and when, and every draw writes its pixels back to RAM before it returns. Think of a shared master file: anyone holding a printout checks the date before using it.

docs.title: Context and Problem Statement
docs.text: The engine keeps host copies of game data: buffer copies, the images draws paint into, and translated shaders. The game can repoint a GPU address, write a buffer from the CPU, or draw into memory it later reads. A host copy must never show what the game's memory does not hold.

docs.title: Decision Outcome
docs.text:
Guest RAM is the one source of truth. Every host copy is keyed by guest-physical ranges, where the bytes really sit in emulated RAM. It is not keyed by GPU virtual address, which the game can point elsewhere.

A MemoryTracker stamps each page write with a global counter, the generation, and who wrote it, CPU or GPU. A copy refreshes when the counter on its pages moved.

Every draw writes its render target, the image it painted, back to guest RAM before submit returns. It also records the counter it left. If the target's pages changed since, by the CPU or a clear, the next draw loads it from guest RAM first. Textures follow the same rule, so a texture that was drawn into shows its latest draw.

docs.title: What this makes easy
docs.text:
• Moved and shared memory are right by construction, and drawing into a texture then reading it is just a read of RAM.
  • A CPU read after submit always sees what the GPU wrote.

docs.title: What this makes hard
docs.text:
• Every draw pays for copying its pixels back, which is fine for demos but too slow for a game at full speed.
  • A small write refreshes a whole page.
  • Depth targets are not written back yet, so a depth target must be cleared before its first draw.

docs.title: Confirmation
docs.text:
The engine tests repoint a vertex buffer address between draws and check the next draw follows it. They also sample a target as a texture after drawing into it, and load a clear that no draw used.

Sources: core/src/gpu/memory.rs, core/src/gpu/engine.rs.

docs.title: Matrix sums copy the chip exactly, written as small loops
In plain words
docs.text: Tensor cores multiply small matrices in one instruction. The real chip adds up the products its own way: in groups, with the lowest bits cut off instead of rounded. Normal float maths gives slightly different last bits, so we copied the chip's method exactly. Written out naively, that makes shaders so big that drivers take seconds to compile them. So we wrote it as small loops and told the driver not to unroll them.

docs.title: Context and Problem Statement
docs.text: The chip sums HMMA products, the half-precision matrix multiply-add, in groups lined up to the largest exponent and truncated. It does not add them one at a time with rounding, as standard IEEE float rules do. A chain of standard fused multiply-adds disagreed with the recordings from a real card. The exact method, written out in full, made each HMMA a shader drivers were slow to compile. Wrapping it in one SPIR-V function did not help, because both drivers inlined it, pasting it back into every caller.

docs.title: Decision Outcome
docs.text:
Implement the chip's method exactly:

Step Rule Grouping Eight products per group along k, four for TF32 (a reduced-precision float) Alignment Every term lined up to the largest exponent Truncation Bits below that are dropped, not rounded Sum An exact integer sum, turned back into a float by truncation .F16 results Each group rounds to a half-precision float Inf and NaN Standard float rules, applied to only those special terms Code shape Four loops, each marked DontUnroll

The inputs are loaded once into a per-thread array. DontUnroll is a SPIR-V hint that tells the driver to keep a loop as a loop. Loop state lives in plain per-thread variables, not in phi values, the compiler's merge points at the top of a loop.

docs.title: What this makes easy
docs.text:
• The tensor tests match the real chip bit for bit on Intel and lavapipe.
  • Shaders with tensor instructions compile fast again on both drivers.

docs.title: What this makes hard
docs.text:
• Intel runs out of registers in this form, so warm runs are a little slower than standard float maths.
  • The speed relies on drivers honouring DontUnroll, which is checked on Intel and lavapipe only.

docs.title: Confirmation
docs.text:
The tensor silicon scoreboard and the per-instruction compile timings in textures and tensors.

Sources: core/src/gpu/sm86/tensor.rs, core/src/tests/gpu/tensor.rs.

docs.title: GPU commands run one after another, each draw with frozen settings
In plain words
docs.text: A game's command list mixes settings changes, draws, constant updates, clears and "tell the CPU I'm done" signals. Their order matters, but the PC's graphics card runs on its own clock. So we process a whole command list before returning. Every draw gets a frozen copy of its settings, everything runs in list order, and the results are in emulated RAM when the call returns. It is like a cashier who rings up each item before taking the next: slower than a busy kitchen, but never out of order.

docs.title: Context and Problem Statement
docs.text: A pushbuffer, the game's command list, interleaves state writes, draws, constant buffer updates, clears and semaphore releases, the GPU's "got this far" signals. The order they take effect in matters, and a host GPU queue runs on its own clock. The emulated OS layer that would wait on fences, the host's done-flags, or syncpoints, the Switch's hardware counters, is still being built.

docs.title: Decision Outcome
docs.text:
Pusher::submit reads the GPFIFO, the queue of command lists, to the end and returns an ordered list of events. The 3D class keeps the raw register words. At each draw it copies what that draw needs into a frozen DrawSnapshot.

LOAD_CONSTANT_BUFFER, which updates a constant table, is an event in the same list. So are compute launches, clears, reports, semaphore releases and acquires. They therefore apply in command order.

The engine runs each event before the next, and Gpu::submit returns once every draw is back in guest memory. An acquire must already be met when it is reached, since nothing else runs that could release it. There are no macros (MME) yet, and no overlap of GPU work.

docs.title: What this makes easy
docs.text:
• Ordering is right by construction, and tests can read results straight after submit.
  • The command reader and the 3D class are plain data code, tested without a graphics card.

docs.title: What this makes hard
docs.text:
• The CPU waits for the GPU on every submit, so real games will need the game's done-signals decoupled from the host's.
  • An acquire that waits for a later release fails instead of waiting.
  • Command lists that use macros fail until the GPU's macro processor, MME64, is emulated.

docs.title: Confirmation
docs.text:
core/src/tests/gpu/fifo.rs for decoding and ordering, and the engine tests for report sizes, semaphore values and acquires in guest memory.

Sources: core/src/gpu/fifo.rs, core/src/gpu/threed.rs, core/src/gpu/engine.rs.

docs.title: The Switch 2 chip decodes with the desktop instruction table
In plain words
docs.text: We read Switch 2 shader code with the instruction table of NVIDIA's desktop Ampere chips. That only works if both chips encode instructions the same way. We checked inside NVIDIA's own disassembler: its tables for the desktop chip and the Switch 2 chip are byte for byte the same. So recordings made on a desktop card test the same encodings a Switch 2 runs.

docs.title: Context and Problem Statement
docs.text: The decoder is generated from the SM86 table, the desktop Ampere instruction set. The Switch 2's chip, the T239, has a GA10F GPU, which CUDA calls SM88. If its encodings differed, every handler keyed on SM86 would be wrong in places.

docs.title: Decision Outcome
docs.text:
Keep the SM86 table. NVIDIA's disassembler, nvdisasm, accepts --binary SM88, and its built-in tables for SM86, SM87 and SM88 are byte-identical.

Compared with the committed table Result CUDA version checked 13.1 Encoding classes, the table's rows None added or removed Bit fields None changed Decoder keys None changed Opcode names Some marked internal, which would break the generated handler names Every fixture word Disassembles the same under SM86 and SM88

NVIDIA's public open-gpu-doc headers also list the T239 under the same 3D class as the desktop GA102 family.

docs.title: What this makes easy
docs.text:
• Recordings from a desktop GA102 card check the same encodings the Switch 2 runs.
  • Handler names stay the public, readable opcode names.

docs.title: What this makes hard
docs.text: • Behaviour is only checked on desktop chips, so equality on a Switch 2 is assumed.

docs.title: Confirmation
docs.text:
The extracted SM88 table is kept on gpu/sm88-table beside a diff summary; regenerate and diff it when a new CUDA ships.

Sources: scripts/sm_86_instructions.txt, scripts/decoder_generator.rs, CUDA 13.1 nvdisasm, open-gpu-doc classes/3d.

docs.title: Real chips are the reference, and known differences are listed per device
In plain words
docs.text: No public document says exactly what every Ampere instruction does. So we ask the chip. We run one instruction on a rented desktop Ampere card, record its inputs and outputs, and require the translator to give the same bytes. Where a Vulkan driver is known to differ, the exception is written down by name, for that driver only.

docs.title: Context and Problem Statement
docs.text: There is no trustworthy public SM86 assembler and no complete description of what instructions do. Hand-built encodings have been wrong before. Public docs and other emulators cover Maxwell, an older NVIDIA generation, not Ampere. Vulkan drivers also differ in float rounding, denormals (tiny near-zero floats) and NaNs (not-a-number results).

docs.title: Decision Outcome
docs.text:
Results are checked against registers read back from real Ampere cards. A capture patches one instruction word into a seed kernel, a small CUDA program built with nvcc that carries the instruction. It runs through the CUDA driver and records inputs and outputs. Observed results are never typed in by hand, and every word is checked with nvdisasm first.

Scoreboard tests replay every capture on each device and fail on any mismatch not listed. Allowed mismatches are listed by fixture id with a reason, either for every device or for lavapipe only.

docs.title: What this makes easy
docs.text:
• It finds bugs no reading of documentation would, such as NaN rules, tensor rounding and shuffle clamping.
  • A device quirk cannot hide a translator bug, because the quirk is excused for that device only.

docs.title: What this makes hard
docs.text:
• Each session needs a rented card and some seeds crash, so coverage arrives in batches.
  • The recordings come from desktop GA102 cards, not from a Switch 2.

docs.title: Confirmation
docs.text:
fixtures_match_silicon, fixtures_match_warp_silicon and fixtures_match_tensor_silicon pass on Intel and lavapipe.

Sources: core/tests/fixtures/README, core/src/tests/gpu/fixtures.rs.

docs.title: Audio
docs.text:
A Switch game makes sound by describing it to the audio renderer service, not by writing samples to a speaker. It lists its sounds, their volumes, their effects and where the result goes. The service then mixes them in small steps. For example, a game plays footsteps by adding a voice that points at a footstep sample, with a volume and a reverb send.

flowchart LR
    V["Voices<br/>One playing sound each"] --> F["Per-voice processing<br/>Decode, change pitch, ramp volume, filter"]
    F --> M["Mixes<br/>A tree of submixes"]
    M --> E["Effects<br/>Delay, reverb, limiter, compressor"]
    E --> FM["Final mix"]
    FM --> SK["Sink<br/>Where the sound leaves"]
    SK --> RB["Sample ring buffer<br/>In the Rust core"]
    RB --> QT["Qt audio output<br/>The PC's speakers"]

How the renderer turns a game's voices into sound on the PC.

docs.title: How does a game use the audio renderer?
docs.text:
The renderer service is audren. The service registry already has its entry, and this design fills it in.

  1. The game fills in its settings: sample rate, frame size, how many voices, mixes, effects and sinks it wants, and a revision number.
  2. It asks the service how large a work buffer that needs, then hands over that memory.
  3. It opens the renderer and starts it.
  4. Every step, it sends an update with the state of all its voices, mixes, effects and sinks. The service answers with their new state.
Renderer fact Value Sample rate 48 kHz Frames per step 240 Step length 5 ms Work buffer Guest memory the game hands over, mapped, not copied Output samples Signed 16-bit, interleaved per frame

Rendering runs on its own clock, one step every 5 ms, and never follows the screen's frame rate.

docs.title: What are voices, mixes, effects and sinks?
docs.text:
Part What it is Example Voice One playing sound: sample data plus pitch, volume and filters A footstep Wave buffer A piece of sample data a voice plays, in PCM16, float or ADPCM, a compressed format The footstep's samples Biquad filter A small filter that cuts or boosts some frequencies A low-pass to muffle a sound behind a wall Mix A bus that voices or other mixes add into "All sound effects" Splitter Sends one voice to several mixes with different volumes Dry sound plus a reverb send Effect Processing on a mix Reverb, delay, limiter, compressor Sink Where the final sound goes The device sink, the speakers De-pop Smooths a sudden volume change so it does not click A voice that stops mid-sample

In the design, the device sink hands interleaved signed samples to the host, in the format the table below gives. The Rust core will keep them in a ring buffer that the C interface exposes, like the frame slot for the display. The Qt window will play them through Qt's own audio output, so the Rust core needs no audio library. If the buffer runs dry, the output plays silence and never blocks the window.

audout is the simpler raw-output service: a game queues buffers of finished samples, and the service plays them in order.

docs.text:
Each game says which renderer revision it was built for, and newer revisions add features.

Revision Adds 1 The first renderer 2 Splitters, a fix to ADPCM looping 3 Longer reverb pre-delay 4 USB output, a higher processing limit 5 Voice decode and flush, performance metrics version 2 6 A biquad state fix 7 Mix updates only when they change 8 Wave buffer loop control, resampler quality settings, float samples 9 Effect info version 2, the limiter 10 Bluetooth output, capture, a second biquad per voice 11 New delay and reverb parameters, compressor, voice drop 12 Filter and mix fused into one step, filters on splitters 13 Compressor statistics, explicit splitter volume reset

On the Switch 2, the renderer accepts a revision marker only the Switch 2 uses. Its work buffer also grew in the 19.x and 20.x system updates. The table above follows the Switch 1 references, so the newest Switch 2 revision is not assumed to be 13 until firmware evidence shows it.

docs.text:
The implementation follows switchbrew's documentation, with the Ryujinx and yuzu emulators as behaviour references only: their code is not copied. Tests use our own fixtures: ADPCM decoding, resampler responses, reverb tails, volume ramps and the final sample format, checked at every step.

docs.text:
Like the GPU demos, the host plays the game's part until the guest path can run a real program.

Distance sets volume and panning. GPU ray queries check whether walls block the sound and pick a muffling filter. Room zones pick the reverb.

In the room demo, occlusion and position are game work: the game computes them and sets ordinary voice volumes and filters. The renderer itself has no 3D audio, just as on the real console.

docs.title: Command processor and memory
docs.text: The command processor is the GPU's front desk: it reads the command lists a game writes and hands each command to the right engine. Memory follows one rule: the emulated console RAM holds the only real copy of anything. For example, if a game moves a vertex buffer, the next draw reads the new place, because every copy is checked against RAM.

docs.title: What does a command look like?
docs.text:
A game puts commands in a pushbuffer, a list of 32-bit words in guest memory. It then adds an entry to the GPFIFO, a ring of pointers to those lists. Each command starts with a header word saying which register to write, on which engine, and how many data words follow.

Item Bits Meaning GPFIFO entry word 0 31:2 Pushbuffer address, low part GPFIFO entry word 1 7:0, 9, 30:10, 31 Address high byte, level, length in words, sync Header 11:0 Method, the register to write, as a word index Header 15:13 Subchannel, the slot that picks the engine Header 28:16 How many data words follow, or the value itself in immediate mode Header 31:29 Mode: 1 incrementing, 3 non-incrementing, 4 immediate, 5 increment once, 7 end of segment

Low method numbers belong to the channel, the command stream itself. Its SET_OBJECT binds an engine, a class, to a subchannel, and its SEMAPHORE_A to D methods write "got this far" signals. Every other method goes to the class bound on the header's subchannel. An empty subchannel or an unknown class is an error.

flowchart LR
    GP["GPFIFO entry<br/>Pointer to a command list"] --> PB["Pushbuffer words<br/>Headers and data"]
    PB --> HDR{"Channel method?<br/>Number below 0x40"}
    HDR -->|"Yes"| CH["Channel<br/>Bind engines, write signals"]
    HDR -->|"No"| SUB{"Which engine is on the subchannel?"}
    SUB -->|"0xC797"| TD["3D engine registers<br/>Frozen per draw"]
    SUB -->|"0xC7C0"| CC["Compute engine<br/>Reads the launch block and runs it"]
    SUB -->|"Other"| ERR["Named error"]

How one command word finds the engine it is meant for.

docs.title: What does the 3D engine keep?
docs.text:
The 3D class, 0xC797, is the drawing engine. ThreeD keeps its raw register words and notes which groups changed: vertex streams, attributes, colour targets, viewport and scissor, shaders, constant buffer bindings, blend and depth, and the index buffer.

At each draw it freezes a DrawSnapshot, a copy of everything the draw needs. That covers the triangle type, counts and instances, vertex streams and attributes, and every shader slot. It also holds the first colour target, the depth target, viewport, scissor, write mask, culling and blending. The index buffer, the bound constant buffers and the texture and sampler pools are in it too.

Two more things happen at a draw:

  • A draw framed by BEGIN that continues the previous one with the next instances merges into one instanced draw. Instancing means drawing the same mesh many times in one call.
  • The window origin setting says whether screen y counts up from the bottom row, and whether triangles flip which side faces forward. The snapshot carries both, and the engine flips the picture to match.

A constant buffer, or cbuf, is a small read-only table the game hands a shader, such as the camera matrix. LOAD_CONSTANT_BUFFER updates one, and it is an ordered event too. So a cbuf changed between draws reaches the right draw.

docs.title: How is a compute launch read?
docs.text:
The compute class, 0xC7C0, starts compute work. A launch is described by a QMD, a fixed-size block in guest memory. Writing SEND_SIGNALING_PCAS_B makes the class fetch the QMD at SEND_PCAS_A and decode it into a DispatchSnapshot. The engine then runs it, see the GPU pipeline.

QMD field group What it holds Program The shader's address Grid and block How many thread groups, and how many threads per group Memory Shared memory size, shared and local memory windows Constant buffers Eight cbuf bindings Signals Two release semaphores Limits Barrier and register counts Textures The sampler and texture pools Version QMDV02_03 and QMDV03_00; others are rejected

docs.title: How do GPU addresses become memory?
docs.text:
Shaders use GPU virtual addresses (VA), which the game can point anywhere. PageMap turns them into guest-physical addresses (PA), the place in emulated RAM where the bytes really sit. There is one map per GPU address space, and an address outside it is an error, never a guess.

MemoryTracker stamps every write to a physical page with a global counter, the generation, and who wrote it, CPU or GPU. A host copy compares that counter with the one it was made from, so it knows when it is stale.

Fact Value Page size 64 KiB, the big page size Ryujinx uses; the T239 value is unverified Map scope One per GPU address space Host copy Keyed by Refreshed when Buffer mirror: vertices, cbufs Guest-physical ranges The ranges' generation moved Render target, the image a draw paints Ranges, format, size, depth Loaded before a draw when its pages changed elsewhere, always written back after Texture Ranges, texture header, sampler entry The ranges' generation moved Depth target The draw's depth address Kept on the host only; it must be cleared before its first draw Translated shader Hash of shader header and code Never, the key is the content

The rule: guest memory is the authority. Every GPU result is written back before submit returns. A colour target whose pages changed outside its own draws is loaded from guest memory before the next draw. A clear that no draw uses is written into guest memory, where the next draw loads it. So drawing into an image and then sampling it as a texture shows the latest draw. Repointing a VA changes what the next draw reads.

Why: keying by physical page stays right when memory is remapped or shared. And nothing can show a frame the guest's memory does not hold. See ADR-0004.

docs.title: What do semaphores and reports write?
docs.text:
A semaphore release writes a value to memory, so the CPU can see how far the GPU got. A report is the same kind of write, asked for by the 3D class. An acquire is the other side: it waits until a memory word reaches a value.

Command What lands in guest memory Semaphore release One 32-bit word Short report One 32-bit word Full report The 64-bit value and a 64-bit timestamp in nanoseconds Acquire Nothing; it is checked against the word in memory

Commands run one after another here, so nothing else could release a waiting acquire. An acquire is therefore checked at once, and one that is not already met is a named error.

docs.title: CPU and shared memory
docs.text:
The CPU side runs the game's ARM code on eight emulated cores that all see one block of memory. The GPU now reads and writes that same block, so a value a core stores is what the next draw reads. For example, a core writes three vertices into memory, the GPU draws the triangle, and the core then reads back the report the GPU wrote.

    subgraph Cores["Eight emulated cores, one Unicorn instance each"]
        C0["Core 0<br/>Runs ARM code"]
        CN["Cores 1 to 7<br/>Same"]
    end
    C0 -->|"Reads and writes"| RAM[("Guest RAM<br/>One block, shared")]
    CN -->|"Reads and writes"| RAM
    C0 -.->|"Write hook on GPU pages"| DIRTY["Written-page bits<br/>Which pages the CPU changed"]
    DIRTY --> GPU["GPU engine<br/>Refreshes its copies of those pages"]

    TURN["The turn lock<br/>CPU or GPU, never both"] -.- RAM

How the cores, the GPU and the planned kernel layer share one memory block.

docs.title: What runs the ARM code?
docs.text:
Unicorn is a CPU emulator library built on the CPU core of QEMU, the open-source machine emulator. The CPU manager builds on it: each core is its own Unicorn instance, and every core maps the same RAM block at guest address 0. A guest address is therefore also the offset into that block.

CPU fact Value Cores 8 Guest RAM 12 GiB, one block at guest address 0 Address policy Guest virtual address equals physical address, no MMU yet Stack per core Starts at the top of RAM, 1 MiB lower per core Instruction set AArch64, the 64-bit ARM set

docs.title: How do the CPU and the GPU share memory?
docs.text:
This work is on the guest-path branch. The RAM block is one anonymous memory mapping, GuestRam, that the cores and the GPU both use. Two rules keep them in agreement:

  • One at a time. A lock called the turn is held while a core runs and while the GPU runs. So the CPU and the GPU never touch the memory at the same moment.
  • The GPU knows what the CPU changed. When the GPU maps a range, every core adds a Unicorn write hook on it. A write hook is a callback that runs on each store to that range, and it sets a bit for the page. Before the GPU runs, it takes those bits and refreshes its copies of exactly those pages.

The GPU's own results go straight into the block before the CPU gets its turn back. So a core always reads what the GPU last wrote.

Coherence fact Value Tracking unit One page of the GPU page map Hooks per core One per GPU-mapped range Host writes, such as the test harness Marked as CPU writes explicitly

docs.title: What will the kernel layer add?
docs.text:
A game asks the operating system for things with a system call, an SVC instruction. The kernel layer, planned in core/src/kernel, catches these calls and answers them.

Piece What it does State System-call interception A Unicorn interrupt hook stops the core at SVC, reads the arguments from registers x0 to x7, and resumes with the result Planned Handle table Numbers the guest uses to name sessions, ports, events and transfer memory Planned Memory regions Fixed code, stack, heap and transfer-memory ranges, with their bookkeeping Planned IPC Messages from the guest to a service, see services Planned Scope One process and one thread first; threads and scheduling come later Decided

Calls that are not implemented return an error, never a silent success.

docs.title: What is known about the Switch 2's CPU?
docs.text:
The Switch 2's chip, the T239, has eight Arm Cortex-A78C cores. The table marks where each fact comes from: SB means documented by switchbrew, the community's Switch wiki, and INF means inferred from Arm's documentation of the core.

Fact Source Eight 64-bit Cortex-A78C cores SB 64 KiB instruction and data L1 cache, 256 KiB L2 per core, 4 MiB shared L3 SB Armv8.2-A instruction set with Neon and floating point SB LSE atomics, such as CAS and LDADD INF Half-precision float arithmetic INF Dot-product instructions SDOT and UDOT INF Crypto instructions exposed to games Unknown, needs a Switch 2 capture SVE vector instructions Not expected, INF Pointer authentication at user level Unknown, needs a Switch 2 capture Switch 2 kernel addition Source New calls 0x80 to 0x82 for GPU memory attributes and sharing SB Two new memory attribute bits, GPU-sharable and GPU-shared SB An error from a sync request closes the session SB

docs.title: How will this be validated?
docs.text:
Each fact gets one of four kinds of evidence, from cheapest to strongest:

Evidence Meaning Doc A test asserts the documented value Arm differential The same code runs under Unicorn and on a real Armv8.2 machine, such as a Raspberry Pi 5 or an AWS Graviton, and the results must match Homebrew A test program runs on a real console Switch 2 capture A recording from a real Switch 2

Passing on a Raspberry Pi 5 shows Armv8.2 behaviour, not Switch 2 behaviour. A mismatch with a documented value blocks the Switch 2 profile, and anything needing a capture stays marked as unverified.

docs.title: CUDA
docs.text:
CUDA is NVIDIA's way of writing general programs for its GPUs. The Switch 2 runs the same machine code as a desktop Ampere card, so CUDA programs compiled for that card make good real-world test programs. For example, NVIDIA's Mandelbrot sample runs through the translator and draws the right picture.

The emulator runs compiled CUDA programs through the translator, on any Vulkan device. It can also run them natively on an NVIDIA card through libcuda, NVIDIA's driver library.

flowchart LR
    CU["kernel.cu<br/>CUDA source"] -->|"nvcc -arch=sm_86 -cubin"| CUBIN["cubin<br/>Compiled kernels in an ELF file"]
    CUBIN --> LOAD["Kernel::load<br/>Finds code, constants, shared size"]
    LOAD --> LAUNCH["Kernel::launch<br/>Fills constant buffer 0 like the driver"]
    LAUNCH --> TR["Translator + Vulkan<br/>Any graphics card"]
    SASS["Guest shader code"] --> WR["Seed cubin writer<br/>Wraps the code as a CUDA program"]
    WR --> NAT["libcuda.so.1<br/>NVIDIA card only"]
    TR --> CMP{"Same bytes?"}
    NAT --> CMP

Both ways a compiled CUDA program runs, and the byte comparison between them.

docs.title: How does the cubin runner work?
docs.text:
A kernel is one CUDA program, and a cubin is the ELF file nvcc, NVIDIA's compiler, puts it in. Kernel::load reads the kernel's code, info, constant and shared-memory sections. It takes the chip version from the ELF header, accepts sm_80 to sm_89 only, and finds where the kernel's parameters go.

Kernel::launch fills constant buffer 0, the small read-only table every kernel gets, the way the CUDA driver does:

Offset in cbuf0 Holds Note 0x0 Block dimensions Threads per group in x, y, z 0xc Grid dimensions Groups in x, y, z 0x28 Initial stack pointer for R1 The real card gives a driver address; here the top of the translator's local array 0x118 Memory descriptor Zero on the card, zero here 0x160 on Kernel parameters Offsets and sizes from the cubin's EIATTR_KPARAM_INFO Section read Holds .text.<kernel> The machine code .nv.info.<kernel> Parameter layout, from EIATTR_PARAM_CBANK and EIATTR_KPARAM_INFO .nv.constant<bank> Constant data .nv.shared.<kernel> Shared memory size

Why this layout: it was recorded from the real driver on a real card. So a cubin compiled today runs without patching.

docs.title: How does the native path work?
docs.text:
cuda.rs, behind the cuda cargo feature, wraps a guest program in a cubin made from a small seed kernel. It swaps in the code, parameter area, shared size, instruction offsets and metadata, and keeps the seed's ELF header and segments.

It opens libcuda.so.1 at run time, with no new crate. Then it initialises CUDA, makes a context, loads the module, launches it and waits. CudaDevice::run_native copies buffers in and out.

When it applies: a host with an NVIDIA card and driver that load sm_86 cubins, running compute programs. The translator stays the reference and the portable path, and the native tests check both give the same bytes. Graphics shaders never run natively.

Sprites: NVIDIA-compiled sprite shaders draw scrolling hills and floating sprites, blended back to front, from a host-written command list.

Post-effect: a pinwheel drawn into one image, then sampled as a texture by a second pass that adds the screen effects.

Particles: a compute launch from the command list moves the particles, then one instanced draw shows them.

BoomBox: the model turns on a turntable under a still light, so the shine and the glowing display move across it.

Ray-traced BoomBox: Red and green walls frame glossy floor reflections while warm and cool moving lights sweep shadows across the room.

docs.title: Dungeon
docs.text:
Showcase: a 20-second, 1080p tour rendered offline at fixed 60 Hz, with audio from the emulated renderer. Ray-query shadows, reflections and ambient occlusion run on Intel Arc MTL. Wet cobblestone and rock use ambientCG 2K PBR maps, with layered fire, embers, smoke, heat haze, simulated water, foam, bubbles, drifting leaves, drips, bloom and volumetric torchlight. This is the console-oriented preset; its native Switch 2 frame budget remains unverified.

Realtime preset: also recorded offline at fixed 60 Hz. It keeps reduced versions of the effects, using baked shadow maps, half-resolution planar reflections, fewer particles and fog steps, and a smaller water grid. The preset name is a target, not a claim that this capture ran at 60 fps.

The Qt selector and capture dungeon --quality realtime|showcase select the presets; --raytracing on|off overrides ray queries. The checkbox is disabled on devices without ray-query support. The local Intel Arc MTL and lavapipe (LLVM 21.1.8) both advertise VK_KHR_ray_query; lavapipe runs it in software.

These dungeon shaders use the existing GLSL-to-Vulkan path. They do not measure SASS translation efficiency. The audio continues through audren renderer parcels; recording drains its ring directly to WAV without opening an audio device. The material manifest records ambientCG asset IDs and the CC0 licence; demos/assets/fetch.sh fetches the maps.

Fixed river view, release capture at 1920×1080, 30 frames with the first three excluded. GPU times below are Vulkan timestamp medians, summed by pass across main/reflected draws. CPU frame times include synchronous submission, copies and audio work but exclude writing the PPM file. This shared laptop had other work running, so small on/off differences are not reliable effect-cost deltas.

Pass Realtime GPU ms Showcase GPU ms Translated/twin ratio Native Switch 2 ms Heightfield 0.019 0.021 N/A: direct GLSL unverified Particle simulation 0.016 0.017 N/A: direct GLSL unverified Planar reflection 1.170 0.000 N/A: direct GLSL unverified Instanced cave formations 0.439 1.049 N/A: direct GLSL unverified PBR, shadows and wet reflections 5.591 41.532 N/A: direct GLSL unverified River surface 0.670 9.173 N/A: direct GLSL unverified Flames, smoke and other sprites 0.238 0.322 N/A: direct GLSL unverified Volumetric fog 0.148 0.363 N/A: direct GLSL unverified Bloom, heat haze and tonemap 1.514 1.414 N/A: direct GLSL unverified

There is no measured translated/twin ratio for these direct GLSL passes and no native console trace. Dividing these times by an unrelated translator benchmark would give a misleading native estimate. An under-16.7 ms console total has not been established.

Switchbrew reports a 1536-core Ampere GPU, 12 GB memory and a 102 GB/s memory bus. The local conformance checklist explicitly prohibits deriving scheduler, RT or clock behavior from core count. The brief's approximately 1 GHz docked assumption gives a theoretical 3.07 TFLOPS, or 51.2 GFLOP/frame at 60 Hz, and the reported bus gives 1.70 GB/frame. Those are peak ceilings, not predicted frame times. The preset uses 96 particles per light, a 256×64 water grid, 24 fog samples per quarter-resolution pixel, four shadow rays per contributing light, one short AO ray and one reflection ray on wet surfaces. Ray work still needs a native measurement and sizing pass before the console target can be claimed. Realtime uses 32 particles per light, 128×32 water, eight fog samples and a 960×540 planar reflection.

The other scene documents in demos/scenes list their guest memory layout and the register writes it sends. Every convention not yet confirmed is tagged "(verify)". The shaders are GLSL that glslangValidator -V accepts. NVIDIA's driver compiles them into the SM86 programs the scenes load.

Compiling GLSL on a desktop card gives real SM86 code for each stage. It does not give the Switch 2's shader header or attribute conventions, so those stay tagged until a real game shows them.

docs.title: GPU pipeline
docs.text: A game draws by writing a list of commands into memory and telling the GPU where the list is. The emulator reads that list, collects the settings for each draw, rewrites the game's shaders for Vulkan, and draws on the PC's graphics card. For example, a triangle takes a handful of commands: where the shaders are, where the vertices are, the viewport, then "draw".

docs.title: How does a draw reach Vulkan?
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant RAM as Guest RAM (console memory)
    participant P as Pusher (reads command lists)
    participant C as 3D class (drawing registers)
    participant E as Engine
    participant T as Translator (SASS to SPIR-V)
    participant V as Vulkan (PC graphics card)
    E->>P: Queue of command lists
    P->>RAM: Fetch command words
    P->>C: Register writes
    C-->>P: Frozen draw settings
    P-->>E: Events, in command order
    E->>RAM: Read shader header and code
    E->>T: NVIDIA shader code
    T-->>E: Vulkan shader
    E->>RAM: Copy the buffers the draw reads
    E->>V: Build pipeline, draw
    V-->>E: Pixels
    E->>RAM: Write pixels back
    Note over E,RAM: The display reads the finished image from guest RAM

One draw, from the game's command list to pixels back in console memory.

The words on this path:

  • A pushbuffer is one command list in guest memory, and the GPFIFO is the queue of pointers to those lists.
  • A method is one command: a write to a GPU engine's register.
  • The 3D class is the drawing engine's register set.
  • SASS is NVIDIA's shader machine code, and SPIR-V is the shader format Vulkan accepts.
  • A Vulkan pipeline bundles the shaders with the settings Vulkan must know before drawing.

docs.title: What happens at each step?
docs.text: Step Code Output Read queue entries and command headers fifo.rs Pusher::submit Register writes, each aimed at one engine Bind engines to slots, run channel commands fifo.rs channel Semaphore events, the GPU's "I got this far" signals Keep the drawing registers, freeze them at each draw threed.rs ThreeD::write Event::Draw(DrawSnapshot) Read the shader header (SPH) and code, translate engine.rs module, sm86 translate_program SPIR-V, cached by a hash of header and code Copy the buffers the draw reads engine.rs mirror Host buffers, keyed by where they sit in guest RAM Run compute launches engine.rs dispatch Guest memory pages the program changed Draw and read back graphics.rs VkState::draw RGBA8 pixels Write back and show engine.rs draw, present Guest memory, then display::present

docs.title: Why does submit wait for every draw?
docs.text: Gpu::submit returns only after every draw has landed in guest memory. So any later CPU read sees the result, with no extra waiting. See ADR-0006.

docs.title: Why freeze the settings at each draw?
docs.text: A draw must see the registers as they were when it was issued. The frozen copy, the snapshot, keeps later commands from changing a draw that is still running.

docs.title: Does compute work take the same road?
docs.text: Yes, through the compute class 0xC7C0. A QMD, the block in guest memory that describes one compute launch, becomes a dispatch snapshot (see command processor). The engine translates the program and runs it over a window onto all mapped guest memory. It then writes back the pages the program changed and releases the launch's semaphores.

docs.title: Guest path
docs.text:
Today the GPU tests write command lists into guest memory themselves. The guest path replaces them with a small program of our own. It runs on the emulated CPU and goes through the same steps a game does. For example, it asks the GPU driver service for memory, submits a triangle, waits for it, and hands the frame to the display service.

flowchart TB
    G["Guest program<br/>Our own ARM code in guest RAM"] -->|"SVC instruction"| K["Kernel layer<br/>Handles, sessions, memory"]
    K -->|"IPC message"| NV["GPU driver services<br/>nvmap, address space, channel, sync"]
    NV -->|"Command list"| ENG["GPU engine<br/>Draws into guest RAM"]
    K -->|"IPC message"| VI["Display services<br/>vi, binder, buffer producer"]
    ENG --> RAM[("Guest RAM<br/>Shared by CPU and GPU")]
    VI -->|"Finished frame"| WIN["Qt window"]
    G --- RAM

The path a self-written guest program takes from its own code to the window.

docs.title: Why write our own guest program first?
docs.text: A real game needs a loader for its file formats, threads, a scheduler and many more services. Our own program needs only the parts on the path to the screen, and we know exactly what it should do. Each step of the path is then tested with real guest calls, and the deferred parts can come later.

docs.title: What does the guest program look like?
docs.text:
It is Rust without the standard library, built for bare-metal AArch64. It has its own start code, and it makes system calls with inline assembly.

Guest fact Value Target aarch64-unknown-none, no_std Image A flat binary, loaded unchanged and started at its first byte Load address 0x0800_0000 Stack Grows down from the load address Built by scripts/build-guest.sh, committed as a test fixture

It has three parts on the guest/scene-crate branch:

  • svc.rs: the system calls, with arguments in registers x0 to x7 and the result code back in w0.
  • cmif.rs: an encoder for service requests and replies, laid out as the libnx homebrew library does.
  • nvdrv.rs: the GPU driver's ioctl numbers and argument layouts.

The scene encoders, which build command lists, shader headers and texture headers, moved into a shared no_std crate called scene. The host tests and the guest program use the same encoders, so a scene is defined once.

docs.title: Which calls does it make, in order?
docs.text: Step Calls Purpose 1 Connect to nvdrv, Initialize, open the device files Reach the GPU driver 2 Read the GPU characteristics Learn the chip, as a game does 3 nvmap create and alloc Describe memory for the command list and the frame 4 Address space init, alloc space, map buffer Give that memory GPU addresses 5 Channel setup and AllocGpfifoEx2 Open a GPU channel with a command queue 6 SubmitGpfifo Submit the triangle's command list, get a fence 7 Sync-point wait Check the fence was reached 8 Open the display and a layer, then connect a buffer producer Get somewhere to show the frame 9 SetPreallocatedBuffer, DequeueBuffer, QueueBuffer Hand the frame to the display

docs.title: What is the acceptance test?
docs.text: The guest maps memory through the nvmap and address-space ioctls, submits the triangle command list with SubmitGpfifo, and polls the fence. It then queues the buffer through the binder, and the window shows the triangle. A second frame with changed vertices must show the change, which proves no stale copy of the old vertices was used.

docs.title: How far along is it?
docs.text:
Step State One RAM block shared by CPU and GPU, with write tracking Done on the guest-path branch Guest image, loader and shared scene crate Done on the guest/scene-crate branch; the guest reaches its first system call Kernel layer: system calls, handles, memory regions In progress IPC sessions and service dispatch Planned GPU driver services and submission Planned; the guest side of the calls is written Display services and the binder Planned Guest demo button and the acceptance test Planned

Left for later on purpose: threads and a scheduler, asynchronous events, and domains, which are several service objects on one session. The game file loaders, the full service manager, and thread-local storage beyond the IPC buffer also come later.

Verified by: the_guest_image_reaches_its_debug_string_svc on the guest/scene-crate branch, and the shared-memory tests listed on the CPU page.

docs.title: How does a frame reach the window?
docs.text:
The core never calls the window directly. A renderer calls display::present, which copies the pixels, bumps a frame counter and fires a callback the window registered. The window then reads the frame through the C interface and scales it to fit.

Why: the window redraws only when a frame arrives, and the core stays testable without a window.

docs.title: Why does the GPU work start at the hardware?
docs.text:
A game reaches the GPU through the kernel and the GPU driver services, and both are still being built. So the GPU work started where the hardware starts, and tests write command lists into guest memory the way the driver would. The guest path replaces those tests with a real program that goes through the system calls and services.

docs.text:
